# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

12556 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-29/JUDGE-review.md
# Climb batch 29: the judge's ruling on the merged-diff review

The merged-diff review of climb batch 29 (heads `1d50c6bbbf` before it and `6a654baa13` after its corrections, base `b430f9f428`) did not approve the merged tree. It raised two blocking findings. Both concern rung T's Appendix I entry `revival-numerals` and the gather's box in `ranges.tex`, which claim more of walk than walk does on the merged tree. This file rules on the two findings and gives the repair. It does not rule on the review's two routed findings, which go to the next batch as the review filed them (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`, "Climb batch 29, listed for his review").

## The standard

- The revision form makes the Effect of an Appendix I entry name "each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row" (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", item 1).
- Where a decision says which side is right and the wrong side is outside the work's area, the departure is recorded, and "if the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds" (same file, "When the text and an implementation disagree").
- A changed sentence that says what walk or the compiled path does must be true of the tree (same file, the paragraph after item 4).

## Finding 1: a negative constant at a program's own number type

**Upheld.**

What the review claimed, and what holds:

- The text says a negative constant reaches a program's coercion "as the prefix operator `-` applied to the coercion's result for the natural numeral ..., so a type without that operator refuses it" (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:215-218`). This follows fork C6's default, "the judgement's repair 3, which he took" (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-29.md:369`). Right.
- Walk departs on the merged tree. Two rungs cause it together, and both causes are in the code:
  - rung F put the fold into walk's phase list (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java:130`, `INTEGERLITERALFOLDING` in `interpreterPhaseOrder`), so `-3` and `5 - 8` reach walk as one `IntLiteralExpr` of value -3;
  - rung N's site takes `x.getIntVal()`, signed, as the digit value, and counts the digits of the text with the sign stripped (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java:160-179`).

  The review's probe at `1d50c6bbbf` (`bin/fortress walk`) printed 't 1 -3' for `t: Tally = -3` and for `t: Tally = 5 - 8`, and 'w 7' for `w: Written = -3`. The type declares no `-` and still takes the numeral. Right.
- The Effect names only the compiled half: "the compiled path gives a program's coercion a negative numeral with its sign, not as the prefix operator `-` on the coercion's result for the natural numeral (row~961)" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5194-5196`). Walk's half, row 968, is missing. Right: the Effect breaks the revision form.
- The record side is done in `6a654baa13`: row 968 filed, and row 961 noting it ("Walk's half, through the same fold: row 968"). Right.

The way not taken is to make walk, the fold or the checker build the prefix minus. That is a code change, and the curator holds it as an open fork: PLAN item 75 lists "the fold keeps the operator's reference ...; the checker, and walk, build one; or rows 961 and 968 stand until the switch-over", with "No default on record beyond the fork's, which the landed tree departs from" (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md:140`). Rung C reported its deviation from C6 as a point (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-numeral-checker/REPORT.md:135`, decision 8). Building the minus here would choose a way of an open fork for the curator, so the repair is the text only. Naming row 968 decides nothing on item 75. Either answer leaves the Effect true: a later fix removes the clause with its row.

## Finding 2: a size of 2^31 or more read as a value

**Upheld, and wider than the review found.**

What the review claimed, and what holds:

- P-173 says "a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` (P-40)". The text follows it (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:105-113`, the box).
- Walk reads such a size "as a `ZZ32` up to 2^31-1 and as a `ZZ64` above" (F-140, "A size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` is refused by the compiled checker ..."). F-140 held this before the batch. The review's probe at `1d50c6bbbf` printed 'big ZZ64 3000000000' for `sizeValue[\3000000000\]()`. Right: under walk such a size is not a `ZZ32`.
- The Effect's sentence "a \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, ... (row~486)" (`changes.tex:5145-5148`) sits under "Both implementations ..." (`changes.tex:5127`). Its list of departures names only the compiled half of row 962, "stops with an error that no \KWD{catch} sees where a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter of $2^{31}$ or more is used as a value (row~962)" (`changes.tex:5197-5198`). Right: walk's half is missing.
- The gather's box says "the compiled type checker and the interpreter give a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a value the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}" (`Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:55-58`). This box is a changed sentence that says what walk does, and walk does not do it for a size of 2^31 or more. Right. The base's text already claimed "the interpreter makes it a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}" (the `ranges.tex` hunk of `4978a9b16e`), so the overclaim is older than this batch. It still has to be repaired here, because this batch rewrote the sentence.
- The record side is done in `6a654baa13`: row 962 now notes "Walk reads such a size as a ZZ64 (F-140): sizeValue[\3000000000\]() typed ZZ64 at 1d50c6bbbf". Right.

The review missed a third passage with the same claim. It is in `revival-inference`'s Rationale, which this batch rewrote: "Both implementations make a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a value a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{revival-numerals})" (`changes.tex:2237-2238`; the batch's diff adds this line). The repair qualifies all three passages.

Row 962 is `CONTESTED`: it leaves open whether such a read is refused where the class loads, raises `IntegerOverflow`, or is no `ZZ32`. The repair names the departure. It does not choose among those answers.

## The review's other work

The review committed only under `explorations/` (`git show --stat 6a654baa13`: seven files, all under `explorations/`). Its `fixed` and `fixesChecked` items cite their commits and runs. This ruling does not depend on them, and I did not check them again. No point to report holds the push, and this ruling adds none.

## Decision: repair

Both findings are settled by edits to `Specification/` only. No code, library, checker, interpreter or test file changes. Under the brief, an edit to the specification is a repair, not a landing on the gate. The edits change prose only. No example under `SpecData/` changes, so the gate's verdict on code, tests and `testSpecData` stands. The repair builds the specification once to check its LaTeX.

## The repair

Work in `/home/user/fortress` on `main`, and load the `fortress-repo` skill and its `specification.md` first. Make each edit below with the Edit tool, keeping the line breaks of the surrounding text. "Replace" means: replace exactly the quoted text.

1. `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5191-5202` (`revival-numerals`, Effect, the list of departures). Replace the text from "the interpreter runs the operator of" through "(row~956)." with this:

   ```
   the interpreter runs the operator of
   \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} where a floating-point numeral stands to the left of an
   \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} (row~958), and counts only one of the leading zeros of a
   numeral with a radix point among its digits (row~960); the compiled path
   keeps a numeral's own type at the selector of a \KWD{typecase} (row~963);
   both give a program's coercion a negative constant with its sign, not as the
   prefix operator \EXP{-} on the coercion's result for the natural numeral, so
   that a type without \EXP{-} takes it: the compiled path as a negative numeral
   (row~961), and the interpreter, which folds the constant as the compiled path
   does, as a natural numeral of negative value, whose digit count is that of
   the numeral without its sign (row~968); where a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
   parameter of $2^{31}$ or more is used as a value, the compiled path stops
   with an error that no \KWD{catch} sees, and the interpreter makes it a
   \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} (row~962); and both leave an expression of numerals alone
   as written where the form of its result needs a prefix \EXP{-} or a \EXP{/}
   that its component writes nowhere (row~956).
   ```

   Keep "The implementations depart from the text in these further ways, each with its row of the revival's gap ledger:" before it. This settles finding 1, and finding 2 at `:5145-5148`: that sentence stands, and the list now names both halves of row 962. Row 968's claim is the source for the interpreter's clause (`explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, row 968), and row 962's notes for the `ZZ64` clause.

2. `Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:55-58` (the gather's `\revision{revival-inference}` box). Replace

   ```
   run it: the compiled type checker and the interpreter give a \KWD{nat} or
   \KWD{int} parameter used as a value the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}
   (\secref{revival-numerals}).}
   ```

   with

   ```
   run it: the compiled type checker and the interpreter give a \KWD{nat} or
   \KWD{int} parameter used as a value the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}
   (\secref{revival-numerals}), the interpreter only where the size is below
   $2^{31}$, since it makes a larger one a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} (row~962 of the
   revival's gap ledger).}
   ```

   This follows the form of the boxes that cite a row in `Specification/basic/inference.tex:261` and `:283`.

3. `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2237-2238` (`revival-inference`, Rationale). Replace

   ```
   Both implementations make a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a value a
   \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{revival-numerals}), where the compiled type checker
   ```

   with

   ```
   Both implementations make a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a value a
   \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{revival-numerals}), the interpreter one whose size
   is below $2^{31}$ (row~962 of the revival's gap ledger), where the compiled type checker
   ```

   Then rewrap that line to the file's width. Keep the rest of the sentence ("gave it the type of a numeral before 8~November 2026, ...").

4. Grep `Specification/` (not `Specification-1.0-frozen/`) for any other changed sentence that says both implementations give a size used as a value a `ZZ32`, or that names row 961 without row 968: `grep -rn 'used as a value\|row~961' Specification --include=*.tex`. The hits that state a decision, as `trait-parameters.tex:105-113` does, stay as they are. Qualify any other hit that states what an implementation does, in the same form as steps 1 to 3. On `6a654baa13` the grep finds no hit beyond those three.

5. Build the specification once, as `specification.md`, "Building it", says. If the gate is still running in this tree, start the build after the gate ends, so that nothing runs beside it. Do not read the gate's output. Both `./ant genSource` and `./ant tex` must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and the warning grep of that section must print 0. Then run `git clean -fXq -- Specification`. Quote two to five lines of each result in your report, with the command that printed them.

6. Commit the three edited `.tex` files locally on `main`, in one commit, with the skill's footer (`committing.md`). The message says that the commit edits the original tree's specification, and that it names walk's halves of rows 968 and 962 in `revival-numerals`' Effect and qualifies the two boxes. Do not push.

7. Record the repair in `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-29/RECORD.md`, in "The tests on the merged tree", after the item on the specification's build (`RECORD.md:51`). Add one item that names this commit, rows 962 and 968, and the build's two `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` lines. Commit that file after step 6, also locally.

The repair does not touch the routed items `review-routed.1` and `review-routed.2`. It adds no test (`specification.md`: an edit of the text has no test) and changes no ledger row: the review filed row 968 and noted rows 961 and 962 in `6a654baa13`.

- P-174 **A numeral's own type is the Working Draft's, `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, both below `Numeral`, and its value carries the Draft's four numbers as fields; a program's own number type receives a numeral through its coercion from that type, which the compiler calls once per class, when the class loads.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`); they are fields of the value, not static parameters of the type, and the Draft's explicit-radix variants and `Literal[\v\]` fold into the radix field. The two types replace the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). A numeral type is written only as a parameter type, of a coercion or an operator, never as a variable's, field's or return type, so the library's `pi` and `e` (`Library/Constants.fsi:16-17`) are `RR64`. A program's type declares the coercion inside itself, such as `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, and reads the four numbers; the compiler emits the call with the numbers as constants, so a numeral at a program's type denotes one object per site, as a string literal does (P-171): in his words, "Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser." A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type refuses a numeral. Inside a coercion's body two numeral values compare by their reduced value, so `2.5` and `2.50` are equal there, under `SEQV` too (P-168). Fields cannot make a size static, so the design contradicts the binary chapter's static word width from a numeral's digit count (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1621`, `:1659-1662`), for Appendix I, and drops its `opr ||` with a numeral. Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`literals.tex:141-145`), as an interval type should receive `3.1415926535897932384` unrounded (`:135-141`). The team built that coercion under its own names, with the exact value in the numeral ("ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec", commit `128f313b5b`, 2009), but never the four numbers, and no team word calls the names temporary or final; the design keeps what they built, one type for each kind of numeral with its exact value at the coercion, and adds the Draft's names and numbers. The team's one word on a numeral's value at run time: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). A coercion handed a double loses: a bfloat16 type then rounds `1.00390625000000000001` twice, to `0x3F80`, where one rounding gives `0x3F81`. P-173 weighs the bend of P-26. Walk, before it runs the checker (P-12), converts an integer numeral from its exact value at each place that fixes a type, and elsewhere evaluates it at its default, which walk already gives it by its value (F-74). Walk gaps: a numeral at an `NN32` or `NN64` binding (row 454), a numeral beyond `ZZ32`'s range at an `RR64` binding (row 443), and coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).

POSITIONS.md:103

Walk converts such a numeral from its exact value where its place fixes a type, at a binding, a parameter and a field, so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `0.25 + 0.25`. The specification's literals chapter and the coercions of `basic-lib/numbers.tex:43` follow, with an Appendix I entry, in the revision form (P-96). A numeral at `round`, `floor`, `ceiling` or `truncate` converts into `RR64` by P-173's reading of a tie among `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64`, so one within half an ulp of a tie rounds as its nearest double, not as the rational: `round(2.50000000000000001)` is 2. No line of microGPT changes, and by reading its numerals keep their bits. Why: the Working Draft keeps a numeral unconverted, since "converting it immediately to a floating-point number may lose precision", gives 3.125 "the rational value 3125/1000", has the library coerce a compound numeral to the rationals, and converts a static rational expression into a float with "at most one floating-point rounding error" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-173`); the curator reads it so: nothing is lost in `QQ`, and a float of fixed size takes one rounding.

- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174), or is a numeral type; `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` (P-40). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true` through `QQ`'s `=` pair, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. == explorations/reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md:5-15

## 1. Coherence

The design is one rule: a numeral converts where it stands, into the declared type, else into the machine default. Six cases get two answers or none; each has a repair.

- Undefined: what "fixes a type". Point 1 lists `Any`; the fork review adds `Object`, `Number` and an unbounded `T` (§1.1); the prototype defaulted at all (probe §1, step 2). Repair: a place fixes a type when its declared type declares a coercion from the numeral type (the eight number types; a program's type by point 4) or is a numeral type; every other type, and no type, takes the default. Then `f(3)` at `Number` is a `ZZ32`, and a tuple at `Any` defaults element by element.
- Two answers: "by its value" where the value is unknown. Row 946 shows it: a variable of numeral type reads `ZZ32` whatever its value. Inside `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, `t = x` is such an expression; so is a `nat` used as a value, whose value a template does not know (probe §8). Repair: the default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of numeral type; a `nat` used as a value has the type the Draft gives, `NN32` (`trait-parameters.tex:84-86`), or `ZZ32` (P-40), chosen once.
- Two answers: the fold against the fields. Point 4 reads the written numeral's four numbers; point 5 folds `7/2`, `-3` and `0.1 + 0.2` into "one numeral", which has no written form: the prototype made `1/3` a radix-3 numeral (probe §1, step 3), and a negative result has no `nat v`. Repair: the fold yields a constant with a sign, as the Draft's `IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]` has one (`constant.tex:49-52`): an integer constant defaults as an integer numeral, a quotient to `QQ`, one with a radix point to `RR64`; a program's coercion sees the four numbers of a written numeral only.
- Two answers: a static argument that several numerals fix. `<|3000000000, 0.5|>` is a `List[\RR64\]` if each numeral converts exactly into one instantiation, refused if each defaults first (`ZZ64` into `RR64` is written, P-74); an `if` join likewise. Repair: the narrowest default holding every value, `RR64` where any has a radix point, each converting into it exactly: the tie rule's form (`inference.tex:313-317`).
- Two answers: a program's type with no coercion from the numeral type. The prototype chained default and own coercion (probe §10, decision 3); the Draft says coercion does not chain (`conversions-coercions.tex:407-408`). Repair: refuse, or name the chain as the one exception.
- Undefined: "once per class, at load" as a semantics. For a reference object two evaluations of `c: CC64 = 3` become one object, which `SEQV` sees (`objects.tex:51-53`), and a raising coercion fails at load. Repair: a numeral at a program's type denotes one object, as a string literal does (P-171), or hoist value types only.
- One answer, for the record: `-3` is `-` on a numeral (`lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`); folded, `-2147483648` fits `ZZ32` and `u: NN32 = -3` is refused. `x = 3` then `x` at `ZZ64` converts (P-74), at `NN32` is refused (fork §6.1), point 1's rule. `pi: RadixPointNumeral` (`Constants.fsi:16-17`) is refused by the fifth default and becomes `RR64`. Two numeral values inside a body: by P-168 value objects compare field by field, so `2.5` and `2.50` differ there, as the Draft's types differ; elsewhere both default and are `SEQV`.

### Step 1, the library: `FloatLiteral` apart, its coercions, the float tie rule, the literal `=` pairs dropped

- `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi` and `.fss`: `value object FloatLiteral extends RR64` becomes `value object FloatLiteral extends Number`, which declares its own `asFloat(self): Float` (P-165). It stays an object, not the prelude's trait: walk makes `FFloatLiteral` values through its native constructor `interpreter/glue/prim/FloatLiteral.java` and calls its three glue bindings (section 4.5). An object excludes every type it does not extend, so `excludes { RR32, RR64 }` holds without the clause.
- `RR64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `.fss`): `comprises { Float }`, and `coerce(x: FloatLiteral) = asFloat(x)`, one rounding (walk's `FFloatLiteral.getFloat` is `Double.valueOf` of the text).
- `QQ`: `coerce(x: FloatLiteral) = numeralRatio(x.asString)`, exact: a new private function of 14 lines reads the decimal text into `n / d`.
- `RR32`: `coerce(x: FloatLiteral) = narrow(asFloat(x))`. Under walk this rounds twice; the compiled path folds it with one rounding (step 3). One rounding under walk needs a float parse of the text, which no helper has (`nativeHelpers` has `simpleDoubleArith.parseDouble` only).
- The `=` pairs over the literal types dropped, 15 in each of the api and the component: `RR64`'s, `QQ`'s, `ZZ32`'s, `ZZ64`'s, `NN64`'s, `ZZ`'s and `NN32`'s `opr =(self, b: IntLiteral)`, and `IntLiteral`'s own eight. No `=` pair over `FloatLiteral` was added.
- The float tie rule, in the checker (`impls/Functionals.scala`, `isNumeral` and `numeralReading`): a numeral with a radix point counts as a numeral at a tie and reads as `RR64`. I put it in step 1 because the library change alone makes ties (step 1a below).
- `Float`'s `asFloat(self)` returns `RR64` instead of `Float` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:82`): with `RR64` comprising `Float` alone the checker reads the two domains as equal and asks each return type to fit the other (step 1b below).
- Lines: 5 files, +46 −41 (the library 4 files, the checker's tie rule 19 lines of `Functionals.scala`).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:47
- P-49 **The compiled checker tries a call first by subtyping, without the expected type, and coerces its arguments only when that attempt is not kept.** The expected type is the type that the call's context requires. The checker's first attempt checks the call by subtyping alone, without the expected type. It keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, by coercion if need be. If it does not keep that attempt, it tries coercion of the arguments, with the expected type. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches. Why: in the curator's words, coercion should be tried when there are no matches.

POSITIONS.md:38
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array stops at its store's factory with walk's own error, which no catch sees (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).

POSITIONS.md:62
- P-148 **The checker's speed comes right after its correctness in priority: a rung that changes the compiled checker also makes the change fast.** The rung times the checker before and after its change. It first makes the change correct. Then, in the same rung, it makes the new code fast, without changing which programs the checker accepts or refuses. So no optimization is left to be done by hand after the landing. Why: the checker must stay usable as it grows. Some slowdown is fine, but new checks have made it orders of magnitude slower, so that the checker ran past the time limit of the batch gate's count stage, and rungs could not land. The timing is a smoke test: one run of each tree, to catch a slowdown of several times; a small difference is noise. The `fortress-repo` skill (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time") gives the steps, their commands and what the rung reports.

== explorations/compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md:30-43

### Step 2, the checker: the default at each kind of place, the literal types unwritable

All in `scala_src/typechecker/` (the patch):
- `defaultNumeral` (`impls/Functionals.scala`): an expression whose type is `IntLiteral` or `FloatLiteral` becomes a coercion to `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, or `RR64`, through `numeralReading` and `coercions.buildCoercion`. It is applied:
  - at an untyped binding, top level and local, one variable or several (`impls/Decls.scala`, the four sites the review names);
  - at a parameter that the numeral fits without conversion, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, where the default fits too (`defaultAtUnfixed`): in `checkApplicableWithoutInference`, in its `AnyType` domain branch (a lone `Any` parameter skipped the argument loop), and after inference in the coercion attempt;
  - at a static argument that numerals alone fix: such a parameter's candidate types are the default alone (no context) or no literal type (with a context), a numeral at a bare static parameter takes its default before the subtyping inference (no context), and a subtyping inference that still yields a literal static argument is refused so that the coercion attempt reads it;
  - at a dotted receiver written as a numeral, `(3).zero`, where the default type has the member (`defaultReceiver`); where it has not, the numeral stays, because the prelude itself writes `(1).asNN32` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:812`, `:814`) and `ZZ32` there has no `asNN32`;
  - at a tie (`numeralTie`): each numeral read at its default, the candidates that the arguments so read fit without coercion, then those where only the numerals' positions fit without it.
- The default ranks as no coercion: `counted` (`Functionals.scala`) and `moreSpecificCandidate` (`useful/STypesUtil.scala`) skip a coercion that `LiteralDefaults` made.
- A typed place whose type declares no coercion from the literal type but one from its default takes the default, then that coercion (`viaDefault` in `CoercionOracle.buildCoercion`). This is what lets a program's own type take a numeral (section 6).
- `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` cannot be written outside the library's own files (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala`): "IntLiteral cannot be written in a program: a numeral has its own type only while the checker types the program." A file counts as the library's when its path holds `/Library/` or `/LibraryBuiltin/`; a type is written by the program when its span's file is the unit's own.
- Joins (`if`, `case`) are not built: an untyped binding of a join of numerals coerces the whole expression, so its branches still make literal values.
- Lines: the whole tree 11 files +231 −59 after step 2.

### Step 3, the fold

- `compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java` (the phase before the checker): an expression of numerals alone folds exactly into one numeral, the Working Draft's static expressions (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/constant.tex`, "Static Expressions"; `literals.tex:163-173`): `+`, `-`, multiplication, `/` by a nonzero numeral, `^` by an integer numeral (an integer base takes no negative exponent; exponents beyond 4096 do not fold), and a prefix `-` on a float numeral. A result that IEEE arithmetic could make a negative zero does not fold, so `-0.0` stays `-(0.0)` (`StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled` asserts `0.0` and `-0.0` are not `SEQV`). A result with a radix point, or a quotient, is a numeral with a radix point: in decimal where the denominator divides a power of ten (`10.0^(-5)` becomes `0.00001`), else with the denominator as its base (`1/3`). The visitor's earlier integer folds (comparisons, `DIV`, `MIN`) stay.
- `compiler/desugarer/CoercionDesugarer.scala`: a coercion of a numeral into `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` or `NN64` within the type's range, into `ZZ`, or into `RR64` or `RR32` becomes the numeral typed at that type (`CoercionDesugarer.foldsTo`). Out of range, the coercion call stays, and raises at run time as today.
- `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`: `forIntLiteralExpr` and `forFloatLiteralExpr` emit a typed numeral's constant, `FZZ32.make(int)`, `FZZ64.make(long)`, `FNN32`, `FNN64`, `FZZ.make(String)`, `FRR64.make(double)`, `FRR32.make(float)`, the floats by one rounding of the exact rational (`roundToDouble`, `roundToFloat`: a quotient of at least 56 or 28 bits with a sticky bit, rounded by `BigInteger.doubleValue`/`floatValue`, scaled by `Math.scalb`). == Specification/basic/expressions/constant.tex:39-142

\subsection{Types of Static Expressions}

There are three groups of traits that describe literals
and static expressions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{literal} traits, which describe boolean,
  character, string, and numerals.  For example, the literal \VAR{true} has
  trait \EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket} and a
  character literal has trait \TYP{Character}.
See \secref{literals} for a discussion of Fortress literals.

\item The \emph{constant} traits, which describe values denoted by
expressions composed from literals and operators (described in
\secref{constant-values});
the type of a constant expression encodes the value of the expression.
For example, the type of a constant expression \EXP{3+5},
%IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]
\EXP{\TYP{IntegerConstant}\llbracket\VAR{false}, 3+5\rrbracket},
encodes the value of the expression; the operator \EXP{+} is
used in the static arguments.  When an operator is not supported in static
arguments, \library\ can still encode the value of the expression by
providing a specific constant trait such as
\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}
(described in \secref{pi}).



\item The \emph{static} traits, which describe values denoted by
expressions composed from literals, operators (described in
\secref{constant-values}), and \KWD{bool}, \KWD{nat},
and \KWD{int} parameters; here the type
does not encode the value of the expression, but the value of the
expression can nevertheless be known statically if specific
values are specified for the static parameters.  Also, in situations
where the type of an expression composed solely from literals and
operators nevertheless cannot be described by a constant trait, then a
static trait may be used to describe it instead.
For example, a static expression \EXP{2(3+m)} where \VAR{m} is a
\KWD{nat} parameter has trait \TYP{NaturalStatic}.
\end{enumerate}

\Library\ declare none of the constant traits.
An expression composed only of numerals and operators is folded, before the
static check and on both implementations, into a \emph{signed constant}, which
holds its value exactly and whose kind its operands give: computed from
numerals without a radix point and without a quotient, it is an integer,
written as an integer numeral or a negated one; computed from numerals without
a radix point with a quotient among its operations, it is a quotient, written as
the reduced quotient of two integer numerals; and computed from a numeral with a
radix point, it is written as a numeral with a radix point, or a negated one,
where its denominator divides a power of ten, and otherwise as the reduced
quotient of two numerals whose numerator has a radix point.
Where nothing fixes the type of a signed constant (\secref{literals}), an
integer takes the default of an integer numeral, a quotient the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and a constant computed from a numeral with a radix point the
type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, whatever its value, so that \EXP{6/3} is a
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{0.5 + 0.5} an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}; where a place fixes
a type, the constant is converted into it as a numeral is, with at most one
rounding.
So \EXP{2147483647 + 1} is the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} \EXP{2147483648},
\EXP{-2147483648} is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{x = 7/2} binds the
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} \EXP{7/2}, and \EXP{0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3} is \VAR{true}.
The operators whose result depends on the width of a type, the wrapping and
saturating operators, the bitwise operators and the shifts, are not folded, nor
is a division by zero, nor an operation whose floating-point result could be a
negative zero: their operands take their types, and the operator its meaning
there.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave a constant
expression a constant trait whose static arguments encode its value, as
\EXP{\TYP{IntegerConstant}\llbracket\VAR{false}, 3+5\rrbracket}, and no library
declares those traits.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that an expression of numerals alone is
folded exactly into a signed constant, which takes one of three defaults where
nothing fixes its type: the value that a constant trait would encode in its
static arguments is held in the constant itself, written as numerals, so that a
coercion of a program's own sees only the four numbers of a numeral as written
(\secref{literals}).}


The only operation on literals that produces a new literal (as opposed
to a constant) is concatenation by using the operator \EXP{\|}.
One may concatenate mixed string and
character literals, producing a string literal.
For example, ``\txt{foo}''\EXP{\|}''\txt{bar}'' yields ``\txt{foobar}''.
One may also concatenate two natural numerals
of the same radix, producing a new natural numeral of that radix.
For example, \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16} \| \mathtt{0de}_{16}} yields \EXP{\mathtt{deadc0de}_{16}}.
\revision{revival-string-literals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 states
the concatenation of string literals, which neither of the team's
implementations built.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a concatenation of two string
literals, as of a string and a character literal, is folded into one string
literal before the static check, on both implementations, and so denotes one
object (\secref{literals}).}
\revision{revival-numerals}{The concatenation of two natural numerals of the
same radix is built as written: before the static check, on both
implementations, it is folded into one natural numeral, whose digits are the
digits of both numerals in order, leading zeros among them, so that its four
numbers (\secref{literals}) count them.}

Every literal trait extends an appropriate constant trait, and every
constant trait extends an appropriate static trait.  So every
literal is also a constant expression, and every constant expression
is a static expression.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:46
- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding. The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. POSITIONS.md:102
- P-171 **Two string literals of one text are one object, on both paths, and a concatenation of two string literals is folded into one literal.** P-168's rule stands: strings are reference objects, and their text equality is their own `=`. So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is `true`, also for one literal evaluated twice, and so is `("foo" || "bar") SEQV "foobar"`, by the fold that `Specification/basic/expressions/constant.tex:81-85` names; a string built at run time is not `SEQV` an equal literal, unless Java answers the same object, as `substring(0, length)` answers the string itself, and then both paths answer `true`. Walk interns each literal's text with `String.intern()` as its evaluator makes the string, and its `SEQV` compares two flat strings' carried Java strings by `==`. The compiled path keeps loading each literal with `ldc`, which yields the JVM's interned `String` (JVM specification, 5.1), and `equality.sEquiv` compares the Java strings that two `FJavaString` wrappers carry by `==`, not the wrappers. The specification gains, in the revision form (P-96), a sentence that a string literal denotes one object and one on the folded concatenation. The team's test `compiler_regressions/seqv.fss:22`, `"cat"==="cat"`, passes on the one library as written. Why: every team source that speaks of literals makes equal literals one value: the specification's "Literals are values; they do not require evaluation" (`literals.tex:25-26`), the 2012 restart's "All literals represent value objects" (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/literals.tick:29`), the team's code of 2008 and 2010, and that test; and Java, Kotlin, Scala and Clojure, whose strings are Java strings, give equal literals one object. Detail: `reviews/literals-2026-11-08.md`, sections 6.1 and 6.4, way S-b with its compiled way (i), and way S-d.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The specification's revision

POSITIONS.md:120
- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.

## 3. Against the Draft

- Kept as written: `literals.tex:25-26` (literals are values); `:141-148` (library designers decide by coercions; coercions to integers and rationals); `:163` (`3.125` is `3125/1000`, at a `QQ` place); `:170-173` (one rounding); `variables.tex:75` (the variable's type is the initializer's).
- Changed in form: `:83-129`, the four numbers as fields, `Numeral` the supertype, `Literal[\v\]` and the two `WithExplicitRadix` types folded into the radix field; `constant.tex:44-74`, a folded expression is a numeral, not a constant trait; `conversions-coercions.tex:98-101`, a conversion also where no type is declared, which that list excludes: the default is a rule beside coercion.
- Contradicted: `:132-141`, "not directly converted ... polymorphic ... may lose precision", at places that fix no type: `y = 3.1415926535897932384` then `q: QQ = y` is refused, `r32: RR32 = y` rounds twice (fork §6.1); the restart's `QQ`/`NN` (`literals.tick:25`, context by P-25).

string literals, and numeric literals.  Literals are values; they do not
require evaluation.

\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{false}\rrbracket}.
The literal \VAR{true} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
\note{And these are the only values of those types.}

The literal \EXP{()} is the only value with type \TYP{()}.
Whether any given occurrence of \TYP{()} refers to the value \EXP{()} or
to the type \TYP{()} is determined by context.

A character literal has type \TYP{Character}.
Each character literal consists of an abstract character in
\unicode~\cite{Unicode},
enclosed in single quotation marks (for example, `\txt{a}', `\txt{A}',
`\txt{\$}', `\txt{$\alpha$}', `\txt{$\oplus$}').
\marginnote{This is not true: Character literals include ``\b'' and
``LATIN CAPITAL A'', which do not ``consist of'' an abstract character enclosed in
single quotation marks.  I think it's better to remove most of this discussion and
direct the reader to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.
This section should be about {\bf semantics} of literals:
their values and types.}
The single quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' single quotation marks
or a pair of ordinary apostrophe characters (for example, \txt{'a'}, \txt{'A'}, \txt{'\$'}, \txt{'$\alpha$'}, \txt{'$\oplus$'}).
See \secref{preprocessing-character-literals} for a description of how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within character literals,
for example `\txt{APOSTROPHE}' and `\txt{GREEK\_CAPITAL\_LETTER\_GAMMA}'.

A string literal has type \TYP{String}.
Each string literal is a sequence of \unicode\ characters enclosed in double
quotation marks (for example,
``\txt{Hello, world!}'' or ``\txt{$\pi\thinspace r^2$}'').
\marginnote{Again, I think this paragraph should mostly be eliminated and replaced with a pointer to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.

Here's a sentence I wrote as a replacement:
``A string literal (i.e., a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotation marks---see Section 5.10 for details) has type String.''}

or a pair of ``neutral'' double-quote characters (for example,
\txt{"Hello, world!"} or \txt{"$\pi\thinspace r^2$"}).
\secref{preprocessing-string-literals} also describes how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within string literals.
One may also use the escape sequences \txt{{\char'134}b} and \txt{{\char'134}t}
and \txt{{\char'134}n} and \txt{{\char'134}f} and \txt{{\char'134}r} as described in \cite{JLS}.

(i.e., ``Numerals may have a radix point.'').  Again,
that distinction is primarily a syntactic one, and can be discussed there if appropriate.}

corresponding to various expressible numbers.
Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
(as described in \secref{numerals}).

has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.

have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is
the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).

In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

== Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:12-237

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.
\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
performed exactly at run time?}


A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
	< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.

The type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ relaxes the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ and
includes two extra values, \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0} (sometimes called ``the
infinite rational'' and ``the indefinite rational'').
\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
If a value of type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ is assigned to a
variable of type $\mathbb{Q}$, a \TYP{DivisionByZero} is thrown
at run time if the value is \EXP{1/0} or \EXP{-1/0}.
The type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} includes all of \EXP{1/0}, \EXP{-1/0}, and
\EXP{0/0}.
The advantage of $\mathbb{Q}^{\#}$ is that it is closed under the rational
operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, and $/$.
In ASCII, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}, and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#} are written as \txt{QQ}, \txt{QQ\_star}, and
\txt{QQ\_splat}, respectively.
See \secref{advanced-rationals} for definitions of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*},
and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#}.



\subsection{Pi}
\seclabel{pi}

The object named \EXP{\pi} (or \txt{pi}) may be used to represent the ratio
of the circumference of a circle to its diameter rather than a specific
floating-point value or interval value.
In Fortress, \EXP{\pi} has type
\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}.
When used in a floating-point computation, it becomes
a floating-point value of the appropriate precision; when used in an interval
computation, it becomes an interval of the appropriate precision.

\subsection{Infinity and Zero}

The object named \EXP{\infty} has type \EXP{\TYP{ExtendedIntegerValue}\llbracket\VAR{true},0,\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
One can negate \EXP{\infty} to get a negative infinity.

\note{What about spaces?  That is, is ``- 0'' treated the same as ``-0'', for example?}
Negating the literal \EXP{0} produces a special negative-zero object,
which refuses to participate in static arithmetic
(discussed in \secref{static-expr}).  It
has type \TYP{NegativeZero}.  The main thing it is good for is coercion to
a floating-point number (discussed in
\chapref{conversions-coercions}).
(Negating any other zero-valued expression simply produces zero.)

declaration that a call invokes among them (\secref{resolving-coercion}).
There the numeral is converted into that type, from its exact value:
so \EXP{q\COLON\mathbb{Q} = 0.1} binds the rational \EXP{1/10},
\EXP{r\COLON\mathbb{R}64 = 0.1} the floating-point number nearest to it, and
\EXP{n\COLON\mathbb{N}32 = 5} the natural number 5.
